title: Who Is God? The Quran and the Bible Compared
subtitle: Why Islam reserves worship for the one Creator—and what supports that belief
summary: Islam identifies God as the one uncreated Creator. He needs nothing, knows all, shows mercy, and alone deserves worship. Tawhid, God's oneness, joins that belief to prayer and a life of duty toward Him. The argument is not that one sounds easier than three. It asks where life comes from, whom the prophets worshiped, and what evidence could justify worshiping anyone else.

seo.metaTitle: Who Is God? The Quran and the Bible Compared
seo.metaDescription: Why Islam directs worship to the one independent Creator, with the Christian objection and the reasons for tawhid examined fairly.
keywords: is Allah the God of the Bible

sections.title: One Creator, Undivided Worship
sections.body:
Islam identifies God as the one uncreated Creator. He gives life without receiving it, knows without being taught, and deserves worship without a partner. Tawhid means God's oneness. Living by it means giving worship to the Creator, not to the things that need Him.

The question is not which religious label feels familiar. It is who deserves prayer, trust, and obedience. Why believe that the Quran speaks for this Creator? [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) takes up that question.

sections.title: Why the Creator Deserves What Creation Does Not
sections.body:
Everything people usually rely on has limits. Health can fail, wealth can disappear, and even those most loved need help themselves. They may deserve gratitude or affection, but they cannot be the final source of life and hope.

Islam starts with the difference between the giver of life and those who receive it. If God is the ultimate Creator, His own life cannot depend on something more basic. A being that receives its power cannot be the ultimate source of that same power. This gives a reason to honor a human being without giving that person the worship owed to God.

Tawhid brings this belief into daily life. Prayer and ultimate trust are directed to the source of life, and each person answers to Him. A prophet can be truly great without gaining a separate right to the worship owed to his Creator.

sections.title: A Shared Starting Point, a Real Disagreement
sections.body:
Muslims and Christians both mean to worship the eternal Creator, not rival local gods. Arabic-speaking Christians also use Allah, the Arabic word for God. They disagree about His nature and whether Jesus shares His divinity.

Christian teaching distinguishes one divine being from three persons. Later councils defined that belief, but a later definition does not prove a belief was invented then. Its truth still depends on the evidence. Islam asks whether the prophets' worship and the claims of revelation support that reading. The history helps explain the question; dates alone cannot settle it.

sections.title: What Surah Al-Ikhlas Teaches
sections.body:
Quran 112:1-4 gives four linked claims: God is one, all depend on Him, He is neither born nor a parent, and He has no equal. Together they distinguish Him from beings that receive life, belong to a family, or have others of their kind.

The name al-Samad in Quran 112:2 expresses creation's need for God; [Ibn Kathir's commentary](https://quran.com/al-ikhlas/2) explains that need. A human helper can be a real blessing, but is not the source of the life and power that make help possible.

The Quran also describes what this Creator is like. Quran 59:22-24 joins knowledge and mercy with His rule and power to create. Life is not a gift from a blind force: its Giver knows those who receive it and calls them to act rightly. Knowing that God needs nothing does not, by itself, prove every claim about His character. Revelation gives that fuller account. Quran 7:180 puts it into practice by inviting prayer through God's beautiful names.

sections.title: What the Shared Scriptures Contribute
sections.body:
Deuteronomy 6:4 identifies one God; Isaiah 40:28 describes the everlasting Creator; and Exodus 34:6-7 joins mercy with justice. These are real points of contact with the Quran. Islam's call is thus familiar as worship of the Creator, not the introduction of an unknown deity.

Those passages alone do not settle the disagreement with Christianity. Christians also read texts about Jesus and the Spirit. The [Catholic account of the Trinity, sections 253-255](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_two/chapter_one/article_1/paragraph_2_the_father.html), for example, denies three gods or three parts of God. The Islamic objection concerns distinct persons within one divinity, not a belief Christians themselves reject.

The question is what the evidence requires. Does revelation support this further account of God, or is its call to worship better explained by one God and His human messengers?

sections.title: Why Tawhid Is More Than the Shorter Formula
sections.body:
Three ideas come together here. The Creator needs nothing, which gives a reason to reserve ultimate worship for Him. The prophets direct prayer and obedience toward God. The Quran joins this distinction with His knowledge, mercy, guidance, and judgment in one account of life.

That connection matters in practice. Worship is not divided between the source of a mission and the person sent on it. Love for a messenger becomes a reason to follow his call to God, not to give him God's place. A shorter formula is not always true. But this link between belief and practice explains why Muslims see tawhid as more than an easier slogan.

Jews and Christians also believe in one Creator, so that belief alone does not prove Islam. The next question is which revelation speaks reliably for Him. [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) develops that argument; [Who Is Jesus?](/articles/who-is-jesus) examines the central dispute about worship.

sections.title: Does This Limit God—or Make Him Distant?
sections.body:
A serious Christian objection is that an almighty God could reveal Himself by becoming human. Simply asking how a man could be God does not answer it. Christians call this the incarnation: the Son becomes human without ceasing to be divine.

Muslims distinguish what is possible from what the evidence shows. God's power does not prove that this account of the incarnation is true. It must be weighed against the claim that the Creator needs nothing and the evidence about Jesus. [The Incarnation Explained](/articles/incarnation-explained) examines that dispute.

Another objection is that God cannot offer close, personal love without becoming human. Islam rejects that conclusion. Knowing, sustaining, guiding, and forgiving do not require God to become a creature. His names in Quran 59:22-24 describe care without need. His nearness is a reason to pray to Him, not to turn a messenger into the one who receives prayer.

sections.title: What This Changes in an Ordinary Life
sections.body:
Tawhid frees worship from the demands of status, money, ancestry, and human approval. Each can have a proper place, but none owns the conscience or the door to God. Gratitude looks through the gift to its Giver. Repentance turns to the One whose judgment matters most.

This is a positive invitation, not just an objection to another faith. Islam offers a life centered on the Creator who knows every need and before whom everyone must answer. Sincere prayer for guidance can begin while the evidence is still being studied. Faith should rest on conviction, not pressure or hostility toward others.

sections.title: The Next Question: Who Is Jesus?
sections.body: Islam begins with one Creator who needs nothing and the worship owed to Him. The next question concerns the central disagreement with Christianity: does honoring Jesus require worshiping him? [Who Is Jesus?](/articles/who-is-jesus) examines that question alongside [the Quran's claim to revelation](/articles/why-the-quran).

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Is Allah a different creator from the God Christians mean?
A: Muslims and Christians both mean the Creator of Abraham. Allah is the Arabic word for God, also used by Arabic-speaking Christians. They disagree about His nature and Jesus's identity, not about two rival creators.

Q: Does a simpler belief automatically become the true one?
A: No. Simplicity cannot replace evidence. Tawhid rests on the Creator's freedom from need, the prophets' worship, and the grounds for trusting revelation. The Quran and Muhammad's mission still need to be examined.

Q: Does Islam deny that God can love or answer prayer?
A: No. Quran 59:22-24 describes His knowledge and mercy, while Quran 7:180 invites prayer through His names. Islam denies that caring for creation requires God to depend on it.

Q: Does this article prove the whole religion of Islam?
A: No single opening article does that. It explains how Islam's belief about God fits its worship. The questions about Jesus, the Quran, and Muhammad supply the next parts of the argument.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **The Ninety-Nine Beautiful Names of God (al-Maqsad al-Asna)** — Al-Ghazali. A classical Muslim exploration of the divine names quoted in Quran 7:180 and 59:22-24.
- **The Cambridge Companion to Classical Islamic Theology** — Tim Winter (ed.). Accessible academic essays on how Muslim scholars understood God's oneness and attributes.
- **Christian Theology: An Introduction** — Alister E. McGrath. A standard textbook presenting the Trinity and incarnation as mainstream Christian scholarship understands them.
- **A History of God** — Karen Armstrong. A readable comparative history of how Jews, Christians, and Muslims have understood the one God.
- **Islam and the Destiny of Man** — Gai Eaton. A reflective introduction to the Islamic vision of God and humanity, written for Western readers.

bibleVerses.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.

Before the mountains were born,
before you had formed the earth and the world,
even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God.

Haven’t you known?
Haven’t you heard?
The everlasting God, Yahweh,
The Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint.
He isn’t weary.
His understanding is unsearchable.
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”

God is not a man, that he should lie,
nor a son of man, that he should repent.
Has he said, and will he not do it?
Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?
Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,

keeping loving kindness for thousands, forgiving iniquity and disobedience and sin; and who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the children’s children, on the third and on the fourth generation.”
